title: Where the Next Fire Starts
indexSubtitle: Is an ignition predictable from what the land, the weather, and the people were doing beforehand? Washington State, 2003 to 2020, on one daily grid.

thumbnail.alt: Shaded contour map of Washington State showing green lowlands, olive high ground through the Cascades, highways, rivers, and labelled cities

subtitle: A daily multi-modal datacube over Washington State, and a spatiotemporal model that reads it, asking whether a wildfire ignition is predictable before it happens and from what.

heroImage.alt: Shaded contour map of Washington State: green lowlands along the coast and Puget Sound, olive and tan high ground through the Cascades and the northeastern ranges, elevation contour lines throughout, red highways, cyan rivers and inland waters, and labelled cities including Seattle, Spokane, Yakima, Olympia and Vancouver.
heroImage.caption: Washington from above, with the Cascade crest splitting a wet, dense west from a dry, open east. Nearly every question in this project is a question about that split.

finding.body: Western Washington logged 101 fires in the 2023 season. Sixty-six stayed under five acres. Two of them accounted for **83% of everything that burned**. Fire is rare, its damage concentrates in a handful of events, and the seasonal drought outlook does not tell you which handful.
